item.title: Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago | Kayode Akintola
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease. That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying.

There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths. The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died.

The crisis in DR Congo is following a familiar pattern, beginning with the delay in recognising the appearance of the disease, partly because it is in an area scarred by conflict, which in turn accelerates its spread and heightens suspicion, even violence, towards those trying to intervene.

In west Africa 13 years ago, nobody knew how to handle a disease they had never seen before. Touching the body of a victim, even after death, risks infection, so burial without proper protection endangers all those present. But the arrival of anonymous burial teams, swathed in protective gear that made them look like space aliens or evil spirits, and taking away the dead to be buried no one knew where – often in unmarked graves in the early stages – was equally disastrous.

Instead of seeking treatment for victims, families kept them at home and buried them secretly when they died, making it impossible to contain the spread of the disease. It was clear that age-old burial customs had to change, but people weren’t listening to directives from remote officialdom. It took members of their own communities, whom they knew and trusted, to change minds.

Those people were local faith leaders – priests, imams and traditional healers. As the then country director in Sierra Leone and Liberia for Cafod, the Catholic charity, I observed priests finding verses in the Bible and imams doing the same in the Qur’an to persuade people to change their habits in the face of this devastating disease. They succeeded where others had failed to gain a hearing, and played a crucial role in getting the outbreak under control.

Living in Sierra Leone at the time with my wife and two daughters, we all suffered the wider effects of Ebola. Part of my work was to go into the field to manage burial teams, train volunteers, and provide equipment for protection and decontamination. I feared for my own life. When I got home, I would have to tell the girls not to come near me until I had bathed and changed all my clothing. At one point I feared I had caught the disease. It was four days of terror, during which I had to tell my family to keep away from me.

I know what those tackling the outbreak in eastern DR Congo are facing. There have been attacks on clinics and burial teams, and those suffering this violence often find that they are feared and shunned by their own relatives and neighbours.

But the main reason for the virulence of this surge in Ebola is the drastic cut in aid between the last decade and this one.

Not only is the response to the outbreak falling behind, the funding gap is widening. Medical institutions and charities are racing to build, staff and equip treatment and isolation centres, but the UN warns that it could take up to 12 months to bring this latest surge in Ebola to an end – if the money is there.

The lesson of west Africa, however, is that faith-based organisations have a role to play. Tackling Ebola is not just a medical problem.

Source: The Guardian Science | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

item.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California
item.description:

SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

item.title: Math Puzzle: The longest shuffle
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

If you repeatedly shuffle a deck of 10 playing cards using exactly the same method, what is the largest number of shuffles you could need before the deck returns to its original order?

For example, a silly shuffle might simply involve swapping the top and bottom cards, while leaving the rest untouched. After only two applications of this shuffle, the deck is restored. What about for more complicated shuffles? Note: shuffles are based only on the cards’ positions, not the specific card. For example, you can say, “Always move the top card down four positions,” but you cannot say, “Always move the queen of spades down four positions.”

It will take a maximum of 30 shuffles before the deck returns to its original order.

Every shuffle, no matter how complicated, ultimately maps each position in the deck to another position, i.e., a shuffle is some permutation of the deck. Permutations can always be decomposed into discrete cycles. To understand this, consider the example shuffle given below, where the top card ends up in the sixth position, the second card moves to the top, etcetera.

Follow the card that starts on top. The first shuffle moves it to position six, the second moves it from position six to position nine, the third to position two and the fourth back to position one. So it travels around a cycle of four positions: one → six → nine → two → one. Notice that the cards that begin in positions two, six and nine also travel along this same cycle before returning to their original positions. Following the other cards, you’ll find that this shuffle can be decomposed into cycles of lengths four, three, two and one. Every card belongs to some cycle, and no card belongs to two different cycles. (Every position points to one other position and is pointed to from one other position. To take part in two cycles, a position would have to point to two different places or be pointed to from two different places.)

Every shuffle can be decomposed in this way. The length of a cycle represents the number of cards in that cycle, so the lengths always sum to 10. For example, the shuffle that simply takes the top card and puts it on the bottom would create one big cycle of length 10. The vacuous “shuffle” that declines to move any cards decomposes into 10 “cycles” each of length one.

A card in a cycle of length three returns to its starting position after three shuffles and then again after six, nine, 12, and so on. So the whole deck is back in order the first time that every cycle has completed a whole number of trips around. That’s the least common multiple of the cycle lengths. To make the deck take as long as possible to return, we want to split 10 into cycle lengths with the largest possible least common multiple.

Cycles whose lengths share a common factor waste cards. Cycles of four and six, for example, are both back in place after 12 shuffles, but cycles of four and three are as well, and they leave you three additional cards to play with. So the best options use lengths with no common factors. The winner is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10, which takes 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 shuffles.

Fun fact: for a full deck of 52 cards, the longest shuffle uses cycles of length four, five, seven, nine, 11 and 13, plus three cards that stay in their original positions, and it takes 180,180 shuffles to restore the deck.

item.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

What decides whether the rock stays put, sinks as a small drip or pulls a much larger part of the lithosphere down with it? A study led by researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) and published in Terra Nova addresses this question with computer simulations and identifies three distinct outcomes.

"Dense rock beneath continents does not sink the same way everywhere. Our models show that its size and density, together with the density of the layers around it, help determine whether it stays in place, produces a small drip or becomes part of much larger lithospheric removal," said Dr. Açelya Ballı, lead author of the study.

A heavy root beneath a buoyant plate

When continents collide, the crust can thicken to 60–80 kilometers (37–50 miles), and its lowest 20–30 kilometers (12–19 miles) can turn into eclogite, a rock denser than the mantle beneath it. Beneath volcanic arcs, similar dense rock is left behind when magma is extracted. Rock samples suggest, however, that the deep part of old continental plates is chemically depleted and slightly buoyant, so it may not sink on its own.

The team therefore made this layer lighter than the hotter mantle below and asked whether an eclogite root could still pull it down. Eclogite-driven removal has been widely proposed from geological and geophysical evidence, but what controls its style and size has remained unclear.

Three outcomes: stay, small drip or large drip

The team ran 18 simulations with two eclogite shapes, a thick, compact body (25 km (16 miles) thick, 100 km (62 miles) wide) and a thin, broad one (10 km (6 miles) thick, 250 km (155 miles) wide), sized after fast seismic anomalies beneath the Andes, Sierra Nevada and Tibet, and combined them with a range of density contrasts.

In some runs, the eclogite punched through the lithosphere and sank, taking roughly its own volume of lithosphere with it (a small drip). In others, a section of lithosphere about four times larger sank with the eclogite inside it (a large drip). In the rest, nothing moved.

Shape mattered first: only the thick, compact body produced drips, while the thin, broad body stayed in place under every condition tested. Density mattered next. When the eclogite was at most 70 kg/m³ (about 2%) denser than the lithosphere beneath it, nothing sank; the thick body dripped only at 130 kg/m³ (about 4%) and above. Large drips formed only when the lithosphere was just slightly lighter than the mantle below it; otherwise, drips stayed small. These are model results, not universal thresholds, but they set physical limits that can be tested against observations.

Sinking in pulses

In the models, the eclogite did not sink as a single piece. It split and sank in stages, triggering repeated drips. Volcanic records in some arcs show activity in pulses roughly 10–30 million years apart, which has been interpreted as repeated lithospheric removal; in the Altiplano–Puna plateau of the central Andes, two magmatic stages over the past 20 million years have been linked to it. Multistage drips have also been proposed beneath central Tibet and beneath the Konya basin in Central Anatolia, the latter in work co-authored by ITU researchers.

The new results offer a physical explanation: dense roots may be removed in separate pulses rather than all at once. Because the models are two-dimensional and do not simulate melting, the link to volcanism remains a hypothesis to test against field data.

The findings bear on the central Andes, southern Sierra Nevada and Tibet, where lithospheric removal has been proposed, and on passive continental margins such as offshore Norway and the Barents Sea, where eclogite appears to have stayed in place.

"Processes far beneath the surface shape how mountain belts and volcanic regions evolve over millions of years. By identifying what decides whether dense rock stays in place or sinks, and how much material goes with it, we can better read the hidden processes shaping continents from below," said Dr. Oğuz Hakan Göğüş of the Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences at ITU.

More information

A. Ballı et al., Eclogite Induced Lithospheric Drips: Implications for the Removal of the Lithosphere at Magmatic Arcs and Orogens, Terra Nova (2025). DOI: 10.1111/ter.70008

item.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
item.description:

Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation chemical engineer and food scientist Dr. Jaqueline Moura Nadolny said the industry needed a more objective system for measuring commercial strawberries' susceptibility to abrasion.

"Limiting bruising helps reduce food waste and ensures strawberries meet growing, harvesting and transportation demands," Moura Nadolny said. "Before strawberry varieties are chosen to breed and sell at a commercial level, multiple traits of the crop are tested.

"Strawberry skin resilience is currently measured by a field officer rubbing a finger along a berry once the strawberries are ripe. Although the scale runs from 1 to 9, most strawberries are rated at the higher end of the scale from 7 to 9, which means breeders have very little differentiation between strawberry varieties.

"Being able to broaden this differentiation more would be beneficial to the breeding program."

Moura Nadolny said QAAFI Center for Nutrition and Food Sciences master's student Yen‑An Chen initially assessed abrasion characteristics.

"These included skin toughness, susceptibility to abrasion, resistance to bruising, firmness, surface discoloration and shelf life," Moura Nadolny said. "These characteristics were systematically tested from simple physical manipulation to controlled mechanical tests to see what impact they had on strawberries. This included measuring the force required to damage or break the fruit surface and assessing the degree of tissue damage after impact or compression."

Final-year students at UQ's School of Mechanical and Mining Engineering then used these abrasion parameters to design the measurement tool.

Mechanical engineering lecturer Dr. Tristan Vanyai said the tool measured how a strawberry was impacted by abrasion. "It works by spinning a rubber wheel against the strawberry's skin, measuring force and torque, which is how much pressure they can take," Vanyai said.

DPI senior plant breeder Dr. Katie O'Connor said the tool was promising. "It allows us to identify potential commercial strawberry varieties for our breeding program," O'Connor said. "These varieties could be better suited to new tabletop growing systems or harvesting systems, like robotic harvesting.

"The new device takes a bit longer than the manual way of testing but is so much better and simple to use. It's still a prototype but once we iron out some wrinkles, we have a device we can use."

Vanyai said the tool was proof of the importance of cross-industry partnerships. "Working with external clients gives students a perspective on how their work can really help," Vanyai said.

Provided by University of Queensland

item.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

- Date:

- November 20, 2026

- Source:

- Columbia University

- Summary:

- Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

- Share:

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.…

Source: Science Daily | Published: 2026-11-21 02:35 UTC
